Fresh carrots have a sweet, earthy flavour rarely matched by shop-bought roots. Establishment can be tricky: germination is slow and slugs attack seedlings. Deep, fine, stone-free soil helps roots grow straight and tender; light soil or compost-filled no-dig beds can work well. Sow short successions for early-summer to autumn harvests. Steady moisture, careful thinning and carrot-fly protection make a big difference. Fresh manure, compaction, stones, drought and rough handling can leave roots forked, tough or damaged.

Celeriac, or turnip-rooted celery, is grown for its swollen stem-base. Its earthy celery flavour suits soups, stews, salads and winter dishes; lifted roots keep into spring if stored cool. Asparagus is one of the finest spring vegetables: a long-lived perennial which gives a fresh, delicate crop just when the garden is short of new green shoots. Troubles

Check alliums at the leaf base as well as above ground. Feeding damage, rot and growth checks can look alike. Use sound bulbs with thick necks or splits promptly; store only dry, healthy bulbs. White rot needs particular care to avoid spreading soil.

Bolting
RECOGNISE

A premature flower stalk forms, often after cold or checked growth. Oversized sets can be more susceptible.

ACT

Pinch out small flower stems without loosening bulbs; use affected bulbs early.

PREVENT

Choose suitable small or heat-treated sets, plant at the recommended season and avoid growth checks.

Bulbs split at base.

RECOGNISE

Bulbs split at the base, often after heavy rain or watering follows prolonged drought.

ACT

Use sound split bulbs promptly; they will not store well.

PREVENT

Keep growth steady with watering during dry summer spells.

ONIONS AND SHALLOTS

Set Division
RECOGNISE

Onion sets may form twin bulbs; large sets and growth checks can contribute. Shallots naturally form clusters.

PREVENT

Use suitable onion sets, plant in season and maintain steady growth. Shallot division is normal.

ONIONS AND SHALLOTS

Birds Pulling Sets

Newly planted onion sets are pulled out of the soil just as they begin to grow.

RECOGNISE

Newly planted onion sets are pulled out before they establish. Birds may investigate their exposed dry tips.

ACT

Replant sound lifted sets promptly before their roots dry out.

PREVENT

Firm sets at normal depth and guard with secure netting until rooted. Check for trapped wildlife.

Tunnelled bulbs with 1/4 in. white maggots.

RECOGNISE

Yellow, drooping leaves accompany maggots feeding at bulb bases. Seedlings may die; older plants fail to develop.

ACT

Remove badly affected plants and infested bulbs.

PREVENT

Use insect-proof mesh with rotation. Clear crop debris; sets are less vulnerable than seedlings.

Troubles

Remove affected plants and seek confirmation.

LEEK / GARLIC

RECOGNISE

Orange pustules mark leek and garlic leaves. Often cosmetic, heavy attacks yellow foliage and check growth.

ACT

Remove badly affected leaves and keep plants growing steadily.

Avoid crowding and excess nitrogen; water roots in dry spells and clear infected debris.

RECOGNISE

Onions retain unusually thick, fleshy necks and store poorly. Excess nitrogen or deep sowing may contribute.

ACT

Use sound affected bulbs early; do not store them with well-ripened bulbs.

PREVENT

Avoid overfeeding and deep sowing. Additional feed will not cure a thick neck.

Leek tips turn white and papery in autumn; damage spreads down leaves and may stunt growth.

ACT

Remove badly diseased plants and affected debris.

Troubles
Recognise → Act → Prevent

ONIONS AND SHALLOTS

Downy Mildew
RECOGNISE

Grey mould develops on onion leaves after wet weather, sometimes followed by black sootiness. Growth and storage quality suffer.

ACT

Remove badly affected material. Dry harvested bulbs thoroughly and keep suspect bulbs out of long storage.

PREVENT

Rotate, space well and improve drainage. Avoid nearby overwintered infected onions; choose resistant varieties.

LEEK / ONIONS AND SHALLOTS / GARLIC

Leek Moth
RECOGNISE

Caterpillars feed inside leaves, leaving translucent patches or shredded tissue. Unlike fly maggots, they have heads and small legs.

ACT

Remove infested leaves. Badly damaged leeks may regrow if cut about 5 cm / 2 in above soil; remove the debris.

PREVENT

Protect young plants with fine mesh from planting out, using a rotated bed.

ONIONS AND SHALLOTS / LEEK / GARLIC

White Rot (Mouldy Nose)
RECOGNISE

Yellowing leaves accompany root and bulb-base decay, white fungal fluff and tiny black resting bodies.

ACT

No cure: remove diseased plants and keep contaminated soil off clean ground.

PREVENT

Do not rely on normal rotation: resting bodies can survive at least 15 years. Grow alliums in clean ground.

ONIONS AND SHALLOTS

Shanking
RECOGNISE

Yellowing, collapsing leaves and foul-smelling slime inside onion scales suggest soft rot.

ACT

Remove rotten bulbs promptly; keep them out of storage.

PREVENT

Avoid wounds and waterlogging. Dry sound bulbs well, store with airflow and inspect regularly.

ONIONS AND SHALLOTS

Neck Rot
RECOGNISE

Grey mould starts around stored onion necks; bulbs become soft and rotten. Damp or damaged necks increase risk.

ACT

Check stores regularly and discard rotting bulbs immediately.

PREVENT

Dry thoroughly and store only sound, dry, thin-necked bulbs in a cool, airy place.

ONIONS AND SHALLOTS / LEEK / GARLIC

Allium Leaf Miner

White specks or mines in leaves, followed by rotting; small orange-brown pupae may be found inside affected leaves or bulbs.

RECOGNISE

Rows of white leaf punctures precede internal mines and rot. Cream legless maggots or brown pupae occur inside stems and bulbs.

ACT

Remove badly infested plants and debris; internal larvae are hard to reach.

PREVENT

Use fine mesh and rotation, especially during adult activity in March-April and September-November.

Choose suitable small or heat-treated sets, plant at the recommended season and avoid growth checks.

ONIONS AND SHALLOTS

Saddleback

Bulbs split at base.

RECOGNISE

Bulbs split at the base, often after heavy rain or watering follows prolonged drought.

ACT

Use sound split bulbs promptly; they will not store well.

PREVENT

Keep growth steady with watering during dry summer spells.

ONIONS AND SHALLOTS

Set Division
RECOGNISE

Onion sets may form twin bulbs; large sets and growth checks can contribute. Shallots naturally form clusters.

PREVENT

Use suitable onion sets, plant in season and maintain steady growth. Shallot division is normal.

ONIONS AND SHALLOTS

Birds Pulling Sets

Newly planted onion sets are pulled out of the soil just as they begin to grow.

RECOGNISE

Newly planted onion sets are pulled out before they establish. Birds may investigate their exposed dry tips.

ACT

Replant sound lifted sets promptly before their roots dry out.

PREVENT

Firm sets at normal depth and guard with secure netting until rooted. Check for trapped wildlife.

ONIONS AND SHALLOTS

Onion Fly

Tunnelled bulbs with 0.6 cm white maggots.

RECOGNISE

Yellow, drooping leaves accompany maggots feeding at bulb bases. Seedlings may die; older plants fail to develop.

ACT

Remove badly affected plants and infested bulbs.

PREVENT

Use insect-proof mesh with rotation. Clear crop debris; sets are less vulnerable than seedlings.

Check roots and bulb bases before assuming a feeding problem.

RECOGNISE

Swollen, distorted leaves accompany soft bulbs. Microscopic stem and bulb nematodes may kill young plants.

ACT

Remove affected plants and seek a confirmed diagnosis.

PREVENT

Avoid moving infested soil. Plan a suitable rotation for the identified nematode and its host range.

RECOGNISE

Black spots and blotches develop on leaves or bulbs of young plants; leaves thicken and twist. Leeks are particularly vulnerable.

ACT

Remove affected plants and seek confirmation.

PREVENT

Avoid moving affected soil and seek advice on a long crop break; the fungus can persist for years.

LEEK / GARLIC

RECOGNISE

ACT

PREVENT

ONIONS AND SHALLOTS

Downy Mildew
RECOGNISE

Grey mould develops on onion leaves after wet weather, sometimes followed by black sootiness. Growth and storage quality suffer.

ACT

Remove badly affected material. Dry harvested bulbs thoroughly and keep suspect bulbs out of long storage.

PREVENT

Rotate, space well and improve drainage. Avoid nearby overwintered infected onions; choose resistant varieties.

LEEK / ONIONS AND SHALLOTS / GARLIC

Leek Moth
RECOGNISE

Caterpillars feed inside leaves, leaving translucent patches or shredded tissue. Unlike fly maggots, they have heads and small legs.

ACT

Remove infested leaves. Badly damaged leeks may regrow if cut about 5 cm / 2 in above soil; remove the debris.

PREVENT

Protect young plants with fine mesh from planting out, using a rotated bed.

ONIONS AND SHALLOTS / LEEK / GARLIC

White Rot (Mouldy Nose)
RECOGNISE

Yellowing leaves accompany root and bulb-base decay, white fungal fluff and tiny black resting bodies.

ACT

No cure: remove diseased plants and keep contaminated soil off clean ground.

PREVENT

Do not rely on normal rotation: resting bodies can survive at least 15 years. Grow alliums in clean ground.

ONIONS AND SHALLOTS

Shanking
RECOGNISE

Yellowing, collapsing leaves and foul-smelling slime inside onion scales suggest soft rot.

ACT

Remove rotten bulbs promptly; keep them out of storage.

PREVENT

Avoid wounds and waterlogging. Dry sound bulbs well, store with airflow and inspect regularly.

ONIONS AND SHALLOTS

Neck Rot
RECOGNISE

Grey mould starts around stored onion necks; bulbs become soft and rotten. Damp or damaged necks increase risk.

ACT

Check stores regularly and discard rotting bulbs immediately.

PREVENT

Dry thoroughly and store only sound, dry, thin-necked bulbs in a cool, airy place.

ONIONS AND SHALLOTS / LEEK / GARLIC

Allium Leaf Miner

White specks or mines in leaves, followed by rotting; small orange-brown pupae may be found inside affected leaves or bulbs.

RECOGNISE

Rows of white leaf punctures precede internal mines and rot. Cream legless maggots or brown pupae occur inside stems and bulbs.

ACT

Remove badly infested plants and debris; internal larvae are hard to reach.

PREVENT

Use fine mesh and rotation, especially during adult activity in March-April and September-November.
